versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 7 But when John saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his place of baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? 8 Produce fruit, then, in keeping with repentance. 9 And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that out of these stones God can raise up children for Abraham. 10 The axe lies ready at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.

11 I baptize you with water for repentance, but after me will come One more powerful than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. 12 His winnowing fork is in His hand to clear His threshing floor and to gather His wheat into the barn; but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

context_lines: John now addresses Pharisees and Sadducees coming to the place of baptism. His severe warning shifts attention from public religious identity to the response God requires. Claiming Abraham as their father cannot take the place of repentance. John insists on fruit: a changed life that fits the change being professed.

The fruit picture becomes practical in [Luke 3:10–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/3.htm). John tells people to share clothing and food, tax collectors not to demand extra, and soldiers not to extort money or use false accusations. Repentance reaches possessions, work, and the treatment of other people. It is not merely a claim to belong to the right family or group.

The axe at the roots makes the warning urgent. John then points away from himself to someone more powerful. His own work involves water and repentance; the coming One will act with the Holy Spirit and fire. John describes himself as unworthy even to carry His sandals.

The final image is a harvest being sorted. A winnowing fork separates the useful grain from the chaff, the unwanted material left from threshing. [Thayer's Greek Lexicon](https://biblehub.com/greek/4425.htm) identifies the implement as a winnowing shovel. John pictures the wheat brought safely into the barn while the chaff is burned. The One coming after him has authority both to gather and to judge.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly read the fruit, axe, and harvest as a call for genuine repentance and a warning of judgment. The fire in verse 11 has more than one established reading.

[Wesley's note on Matthew 3:11](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-matthew/) understands it as the Spirit kindling love in people's hearts and connects it with the fiery appearance at Pentecost. The [Catholic Catechism, paragraph 696](https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P21.HTM), likewise uses John's words when explaining fire as an image of the Spirit's transforming work.

[Baptist commentator John Gill on Matthew 3:11](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/matthew/3.htm) acknowledges the Pentecost reading but favors a judgment reading, pointing to the fire around it in verses 10 and 12. The [US Catholic bishops' note on 3:11](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/matthew/3) also discusses cleansing for the repentant and judgment for the unrepentant. These differences cross church boundaries; the sources do not support assigning one interpretation to every Catholic or every Protestant.
god_plan_lines: John's promise reaches beyond his own work. In [Acts 1:4–5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/1.htm), Jesus explicitly contrasts John's water baptism with the coming gift of the Holy Spirit. [Acts 2:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/2.htm) then records the Spirit filling the disciples. The messenger can prepare and point ahead, but the promised gift comes through Jesus.

The combination of cleansing and judgment also recalls the prophets. [Malachi 3:1–4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/malachi/3.htm) describes a messenger preparing the way and the Lord's coming with a refining fire; [Malachi 4:1–2](https://biblehub.com/bsb/malachi/4.htm) places judgment on evil alongside healing for those who fear God. These are parallels in the Bible's account of God's coming, not grounds for inventing a date or reducing every fire image to exactly the same event.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
